paras: The killing of four Mexican prisoners near Dolores, Texas, took place on August 25, 1881, when unknown attackers fired on four men accused of horse theft as their captors carried them toward the jail at Brackett. All four were killed, and an inquest returned a verdict that they had died at the hands of persons unknown. A wire dispatch carried the news across the country, where papers variously described it as "Summary Justice", a lynching and a murder.

According to a Brackett special printed in the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman, a "regular organized band" of horse thieves had for some time been running off stock along the Rio Grande. Some days before the killing, sheep men including McLeod and Thompson were deputized to arrest the thieves, and they overtook and captured four of them. The same account described all four as Mexicans and named one, Tolomantez, as well known in the area "as a desperado and horse thief."

The captors were bringing the prisoners back to Brackett in an ambulance and had come within about twelve miles of the town, near Dolores, when hidden attackers opened fire. All four prisoners were killed, while no injury to the captors is reported. The wire placed the attack on the day before its August 26 dispatch, and a later brief dated it to the 25th.

On hearing of the killing, Justice Maguire summoned a jury and went out to hold an inquest over the bodies. The Dallas Daily Herald reported that the jury found the Mexicans "were killed by persons unknown." No report of an arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The first notice was a short wire dispatch from Brackett, printed from August 26 in papers from Dakota Territory to California under heads such as "Horse Thieves Killed" and "Four Horse-Thieves Killed." The Eureka Daily Sentinel ran it as "Summary Justice," and versions garbled the place as "Daleres" or "Dallas." The wire named neither victims nor attackers and did not mention race.

Texas papers added the detail: the Austin special identified the victims as Mexicans, named the captors and one victim, and called the prisoners "rascals" and their captors "gentlemen." The Dallas Daily Herald used the word "murdered" and reported only that the captors "claim" a crowd had done the killing. In the weekly digests of early September, the story became "lynched" in Connecticut, "taken from officers ... and put to death" in Wisconsin and "A mob killed" in Illinois. A separate digest line, reprinted in Arkansas, Kansas, Missouri and other states, said the four were "shot dead while making off with valuable stock."

Accounts differ on the circumstances: the Brackett dispatch and both Texas papers place the prisoners in their captors' custody when they were shot, while the digest line has them killed in the act of driving off stock. The identity of the attackers also rests on differing words, "hidden parties" in the Austin special and a "crowd" in the captors' own claim as reported from Dallas.

reader.title: Killing of four Mexican prisoners near Dolores, Texas
bases: Four prisoners accused of horse theft were shot dead by unknown attackers while being taken to jail by deputized captors (A1, A9), an act a Texas paper called murder and northern briefs called a lynching (A8, A10, A13).

Four prisoners were killed without legal process by 'hidden parties' who fired on their captors' wagon (A9), and the inquest found them killed by persons unknown (A8). The attackers' number is not given beyond plural 'parties', a 'crowd' in the captors' claim and 'a mob' in one brief (A8, A9, A13), and no motive is stated, though the victims were accused horse thieves (A9).

The wire (A1), an Austin special from Brackett (A9) and a Dallas item reporting the inquest (A8) agree that four prisoners were killed near Dolores, though a digest version (A7) has the four shot while making off with stock.

accounts.label: Brackett wire
accounts.gist: Four horse thieves of a long-operating Rio Grande gang, being brought to Brackett in officers' charge, were attacked near Dolores and all killed.

accounts.label: Brackett special to the Austin Statesman
accounts.gist: Deputized sheep men McLeod and Thompson captured four Mexicans and were bringing them in an ambulance when 'hidden parties' fired from cover about twelve miles out and killed all four; the justice went out to hold an inquest.

accounts.label: Captors' claim, as reported in Dallas
accounts.gist: McLoed and Thompson 'claim' a crowd killed the prisoners; the inquest jury found the killers to be persons unknown.

accounts.label: Weekly digest version
accounts.gist: Four Mexican horse thieves were shot dead while making off with valuable stock near Brackett, with no mention of capture or custody.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire under heads such as 'Horse Thieves Killed', 'Four Horse-Thieves Killed' and 'Summary Justice', without comment on the attackers.
The Dallas Daily Herald wrote that the Mexicans were 'murdered' and that the captors 'claim' a crowd did it.
The Austin special called the prisoners 'rascals' and a dead man a known 'desperado and horse thief', while calling the captors 'gentlemen'.
Northern digests condensed it to 'lynched', 'taken from officers ... and put to death' and 'A mob killed'.

conflicts.note: The custody version comes from the Brackett dispatch and two Texas papers, one reporting the inquest; the stock-raid version is an unsourced digest line.

versions.value: Hidden parties who fired from cover

conflicts.note: The Dallas paper presents the crowd version as the captors' claim; the inquest named no one.
The killing itself is placed on the 25th ('yesterday' from the 26th; 'on the 25th').
